title: Any wild species domesticated as long would vary as much as existing domestics

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Any wild species domesticated as long would vary as much as existing domestics

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Domesticated species were not chosen for an unusual inherent tendency to vary; any comparable set of wild animals and plants, bred under domestication for as many generations, would on average vary as much as the parent species of existing domesticated productions have.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: I cannot doubt that if other animals and plants, equal in number to our domesticated productions, and belonging to equally diverse classes and countries, were taken from a state of nature, and could be made to breed for an equal number of generations under domestication, they would vary on an average as largely as the parent species of our existing domesticated productions have varied.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter I, “Variation under Domestication”; section “Origin of Domestic Varieties from one or more Species”. Scope: wild animals and plants brought into domestication

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch01-08: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.37

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The prediction is measurable but explicitly requires long, matched domestication experiments on a representative set of wild species. Existing domestication episodes are selected, heterogeneous and too few for the proposed counterfactual.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Randomly sample many wild species across clades, maintain them under comparable domestication for the same number of generations, and compare standardized heritable variance with established domestic progenitors. Comparable mean variance would support the prediction.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The required counterfactual domestication histories do not exist.

Survivorship and domestication feasibility would bias species selection.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.44
operationalizability: 0.69
data existence: 0.28
analysis feasibility: 0.3
data adequacy: 0.13

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The prediction is clear enough to score once generation depth and taxonomic spread are matched. That matched series does not exist in any open database, and a few recent domestication genome projects are not a substitute for it. Resolving the counterfactual would require new long-running breeding records rather than a reanalysis of current archives.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Domesticate a matched set of previously wild species, equal in number, taxonomic spread, and generations to existing domesticated productions, and compare their accumulated phenotypic variance. Equal average variance would support the prediction; systematically less variance in the new domesticates, after matching generations and diversity of conditions, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Variance under domestication confounds generations of breeding with intentional selection intensity.

No public experiment has kept a taxonomically matched set of wild species under domestication for a number of generations comparable to ancient crops and livestock.

Recent domestications such as farmed fish differ in breeding intensity and are documented case by case.

discriminating power: 0.34
